p.src: Strangely enough, I had taken a liking to Gael, the president of a glass company. Gael was the capitalist of capitalists. Among all the kappas in that country, there surely could not have been another with a belly as large as Gael's. Yet when he sat in an easy chair with his lychee-like wife on one side and his cucumber-like child on the other, he looked almost like happiness itself. From time to time, Judge Pep and Dr. Chak took me to dinner at Gael's house. Armed with a letter of introduction from Gael, I also toured various factories in which he and his friends had some interest. Of all those factories, the one I found especially interesting belonged to a book-manufacturing company. When I entered this factory with a young kappa engineer and saw its enormous hydroelectric-powered machinery, I was struck anew by the progress of mechanical industry in the land of the kappas. I was told that it produced seven million copies of books a year. But it was not the number of books that astonished me. It was how little effort was required to produce so many. For in this country, making books required nothing more than feeding paper, ink, and a gray powder into the funnel-shaped mouth of a machine. Once these raw materials entered the machine, in less than five minutes they emerged as countless books in crown, duodecimo, half-crown, and other formats. As I watched books of every kind pour down like a waterfall, I asked the kappa engineer, who stood leaning backward, what the gray powder was called. The engineer remained standing before the machine, which gleamed with a black sheen, and replied with an air of boredom: “This? This is donkey brain.

p.src: Of course, industrial miracles of this kind were not confined to book-manufacturing companies. The same thing was happening at painting-manufacturing and music-manufacturing companies as well. Indeed, according to Gael, an average of seven or eight hundred new kinds of machines were invented in that country every month, and everything was being mass-produced at a tremendous pace without any need for human labor. Consequently, no fewer than forty or fifty thousand workers were dismissed as well. And yet, though I read the newspaper every morning in that country, I never once encountered the word “strike.” This struck me as strange, so when I was once again invited with Pep and Chak to dine at Gael's house, I took the opportunity to ask why. “They eat them all, you see.” With an after-dinner cigar between his lips, Gael said this as casually as could be. But I had no idea what he meant by “eat them.” Chak, who wore pince-nez, seemed to notice my bewilderment and offered an explanation from beside me. “They kill all those workers and use their flesh as food. Take a look at this newspaper here. Exactly 64,769 workers were dismissed this month, so the price of meat has fallen accordingly.” “Do the workers simply let themselves be killed without protest?” “There is no use making a fuss. After all, we have the Worker Slaughter Act.” These were the words of Pep, who sat looking bitter with a potted wax myrtle behind him. Naturally, I was disgusted. But not only our host Gael, but Pep and Chak as well, seemed to regard the whole thing as perfectly natural. Indeed, Chak addressed me with a laugh and a mocking air: “In short, the state saves them the trouble of starving to death or committing suicide.

p.src: “But to eat their flesh—” “You mustn’t talk such nonsense. If Magg heard you, he would surely roar with laughter. In your country too, do not the daughters of the Fourth Estate become prostitutes? To be outraged over something like eating the flesh of workers is mere sentimentalism.” Gael, who had been listening to this exchange, offered me a plate of sandwiches from a nearby table and said to me with perfect composure: “Well? Won’t you have one? These are made of workers’ flesh too, you know.” Naturally, I recoiled in horror. No, that was not all. Leaving the laughter of Pepp and Chack behind me, I fled from the drawing room of Gael’s house. It happened to be a stormy night, without even a glimmer of starlight above the houses. As I made my way through the darkness back to my lodgings, I vomited without cease. Vomit that streamed ghostly white even in the darkness of night.
